english: We've been friends for ten years.
tip: 된 (doen) after a length of time means 'that has lasted that long': 십 년 된 친구 (sip nyeon doen chingu) = a friend of ten years' standing.

english: I don't have many close friends.
tip: 많지 않아요 (manchi anayo) = 'not many' – the long -지 않다 (-ji anta) negation. Short 안 (an) works too: 안 많아요 (an manayo). Same meaning; the long form is a touch more formal.

target: 친구가 힘들어할 때 옆에서 위로해 줬어요.
english: I comforted my friend when they were struggling.
tip: 3rd-person feelings take -어하다: 친구가 힘들어해요 (himdeureohaeyo), not 힘들어요.

target: 저는 새 친구를 쉽게 못 사귀어요.
english: I don't make new friends easily.
tip: 못 (mot) before a verb means 'can't', not 'don't': 못 사귀어요 (mot sagwieoyo) = can't make (friends). 안 (an) would claim you choose not to.

english: We got close quickly because our hobbies are similar.
tip: -아/어서 glues 'because' straight onto the verb: 비슷해서 (biseuthaeseo) = because they're similar – cause first, result after, no separate word for 'because'.

target: 저는 친구의 비밀을 끝까지 지켜 줬어요.
english: I kept my friend's secret to the end.
tip: Adding 주다 (juda = give) after a verb marks it as done for someone's benefit: 지켜 줬어요 (jikyeo jwosseoyo) = kept it as a favor to my friend, not just kept it.

english: We tell each other everything.
tip: -든지 turns question words into any-words: 뭐든지 (mwodeunji) = anything, 누구든지 (nugudeunji) = anyone, 언제든지 (eonjedeunji) = anytime. One suffix, a whole series.

english: I chatted with a friend all night.
tip: You don't 'have' a chat in Korean – you shake one: 수다를 떨다 (suda-reul tteolda), where 떨다 (tteolda) means shake or rattle. 떨었어요 (tteoreosseoyo) = chattered away.

target: 그 친구랑은 말이 정말 잘 통해요.
english: I click really well with that friend.
tip: 말이 통해요 (mari tonghaeyo) is literally 'words get through' – 통하다 (tonghada) means to flow or pass through. Clicking with someone = your words flow freely.

target: 두 사람이 요즘 사귀는 것 같아요.
english: Those two seem to be dating these days.
tip: -는 것 같아요 (-neun geot gatayo) = 'it seems that': a soft guess.

english: I fell for that person at first sight.
tip: 첫눈에 반했어요 (cheonnune banhaesseoyo) = fell for them 'at first eye': 첫눈 (cheonnun) is literally 'first eye/glance'. Same idea as English's first sight, built from the eye.

english: We started dating last month.
tip: 시작하다 (sijakhada = start) needs a noun, so -기 turns the verb into one: 사귀기 시작했어요 (sagwigi sijakhaesseoyo) = started dating, literally 'started the dating'.

english: He likes her a lot.
tip: 좋아하다 (joahada) is a true verb, so you can say it about anyone: 그는 좋아해요 (geuneun joahaeyo) = he likes. Plain feeling adjectives can't describe a third person that directly.

english: I was so nervous on the first date.
tip: 긴장됐어요 (ginjangdwaesseoyo) is built on 되다 (doeda = become): nerves are something that happens to you in Korean, not a state you are.

english: I talk on the phone with my girlfriend every night.
tip: Korean splits phoning: 전화하다 (jeonhwahada) = place the call, 통화하다 (tonghwahada) = have the conversation. Nightly 통화해요 (tonghwahaeyo) means real talks, not dialing.

english: It's our 100-day anniversary next week.
tip: 백일 (baegil) = the 100-day mark couples celebrate.

english: I keep thinking about that person.
tip: In 생각이 나요 (saenggagi nayo) the thought is the subject: it 'comes up' on its own – 나다 (nada) = arise. You're not doing the thinking; the person keeps surfacing in your head.

english: I haven't confessed my feelings yet.
tip: -지 못하다 is the long form of 못 (mot = can't): 고백하지 못했어요 (gobaekhaji mothaesseoyo) = haven't been able to confess – inability, not just 'didn't'.

english: I think you get comfortable after dating a long time.
tip: -(으)면 covers both 'if' and 'when' in one ending: 사귀면 (sagwimyeon) = if/once you date. English forces a choice between the two; Korean leaves it to context.

english: Work matters more to me than dating.
tip: -보다 (boda = than) attaches straight to the thing compared: 연애보다 (yeonaeboda) = than dating. The order flips English: 'than dating, work is more important'.

english: We walked in the park holding hands.
tip: -고 chains actions and only the last verb takes the tense: 잡고 걸었어요 (japgo georeosseoyo) = held and walked – 잡고 stays bare, 걸었어요 carries the past for both.

english: My parents oppose my career path.
tip: Elders as subject take -세요: 부모님은 반대하세요 (bandaehaseyo).

target: 어머니께서 제 성적 때문에 화가 나셨어요.
english: My mother got angry about my grades.
tip: 께서 (kkeseo) is the respect version of the subject marker, and the verb matches with -시-: 어머니께서 나셨어요 (eomeonikkeseo nasyeosseoyo). Respect is marked twice – noun and verb.

english: My father doesn't like my friends.
tip: Honorific negation: 좋아하지 않으세요 (joahaji aneuseyo).

english: It's hard for me to speak honestly to my parents.
tip: 한테 (hante = to) upgrades to 께 (kke) when the receiver is respected: 부모님께 (bumonimkke) = to my parents. The particle alone signals the respect, before the verb does.

english: This time I'll apologize first.
tip: 사과할게요 (sagwahalgeyo) is not plain future: -(으)ㄹ게요 makes it a promise to the listener – 'I'll apologize, count on it'. It only works with someone there to hear it.

english: I won't say things like that again.
tip: 다시는 (dasineun) with a negative means 'never again': 하지 않을게요 (haji aneulgeyo) = I promise not to do it – together, a never-again promise with the 'ever' built in.

english: I told my father I was sorry.
tip: 말씀드리다 (malsseumdeurida) = humbly 'tell' an elder.

english: My mother understood my feelings.
tip: 주다 (juda) marks a favor; it becomes 주시다 (jusida) when the favor-doer is honored: 이해해 주셨어요 (ihaehae jusyeosseoyo) = she kindly understood – respect for mom built into the verb.

english: The bride was truly beautiful.
tip: Inner feelings need -어하다 when said of others, but looks are visible to all, so 아름답다 (areumdapda) stays plain: 아름다웠어요 (areumdawosseoyo) = she was beautiful.
